::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Compute the sum of an exponent divided by factorial](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2243696/compute-the-sum-of-an-exponent-divided-by-factorial), asked by [Denis Kulagin](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/142444/denis-kulagin) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2017-04-20; [CC BY-SA 3.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/)):

> There was much discussion on Math SO why
>
> $$\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{\alpha^n}{n!}  = 0$$
>
> when $\alpha > 1$. What would be the strategy for computing:
>
> $$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{\alpha^n}{n!}$$
>
> given that it's convergence is easlity proven using *ratio test*.
:::

The power series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}$ converges for all $x$.  If we call it by $f(x)$, notice that
$$f'(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{nx^{n-1}}{n!}
          = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{x^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}
          = \sum_{m=0}^\infty \frac{x^{m}}{m!} = f(x)$$
Also, $f(0) = 1$.  These two properties characterize the exponential function, by uniqueness of solutions to ordinary differential equations.  Therefore $f(x) = e^x$ for all $x$.
